MILWAUKEE — A new Marquette Law School Poll of Wisconsin finds that, in the race for governor, Democrat David Crowley is supported by 49% of likely voters and Republican Tom Tiffany is supported by 46%, with 5% undecided.
Among all registered voters, Crowley is the choice of 46%, and Tiffany is supported by 45%, with 9% undecided.
In August, Crowley had 49% and Tiffany 44% among likely voters, and the race was tied with 44% each among registered voters.
Partisans are strongly behind their nominees, with 95% of Republicans backing Tiffany and 96% of Democrats for Crowley among likely voters.
Independents strongly favor Crowley, with 44% supporting him and 18% supporting Tiffany, but a large 38% are undecided.
Results among registered voters are similar, with a few more voters undecided.
Compared to August, Republican support for Tiffany increased by 4 percentage points, while Democratic support for Crowley slipped by 2 points.
Independent support for Crowley fell by 11 points.
The percentage of independents voting for Tiffany rose by 2 points, while the percentage of independents who are undecided rose by 8 points.
All these figures are among likely voters.

The final fundraising reports in the race for governor show Democratic billionaires are helping give Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley a late fundraising edge over Republican U.S.
Rep.
Tom Tiffany and the GOP billionaires backing him.
The latest numbers stand out because Tiffany had previously outraised Crowley nearly 2-1 throughout the campaign.
Filings with the Wisconsin Ethics Commission show Crowley raked in around $15.5 million between July 1 and Oct.
19, while Tiffany raised around $10 million.
The lion’s share of the money going to campaigns came by way of transfers from state parties, which face no limits on how much they can accept from wealthy donors or how much they can give to candidates.
Crowley received $11.4 million in transfers during the reporting period from the Democratic Party of Wisconsin, which reported getting $5.5 million from LinkedIn founder Reid Hoffman; $2 million from former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg; $1.5 million from philanthropist Lynn Schusterman; and $1 million each from philanthropists Nina Singh Wanstrath and Lynde Uihlein.
Tiffany reported around $9 million in transfers from the Republican Party of Wisconsin, which got a single $13 million donation from GOP megadonor Diane Hendricks.
In the latest reporting period, Hendricks was one of just six donors to the state Republican Party, accounting for nearly all of the party’s fundraising haul from individual donors.

Prior to report, Republicans dominated fundraising
Before the uptick for Democrats in the latest report, Tiffany had dominated Crowley in fundraising in 2026.
Since Jan.
1, Tiffany has raised nearly $50 million compared around $27 million raised by Crowley.
Tiffany spent about $47 million over the course of the calendar year compared to about $23 million for Crowley.
The Democratic and Republican parties had seen similar gaps.
The state GOP reported bringing in more than $57 million throughout 2026.
That’s more than twice state Democrats’ haul of around $28 million.
That gap narrowed in the latest finance reports, which showed both parties raised around $15 million since July 1 when all transfers were factored in.
All told this year, Hendricks has donated more than $23 million to the Republican Party, and fellow conservative billionaires Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein have contributed a total of more than $32 million.
Hoffman has been the state Democratic Party’s biggest donor in 2026, giving more than $8.75 million.
In addition to the recent donations from Bloomberg, Schusterman, Wanstrath and Lynde Uihlein, Democratic Illinois Gov.
JB Pritzker gave $1 million to the Democratic Party of Wisconsin shortly after Crowley won the primary.

The 2026 United States Senate election in Nebraska will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the United States Senate to represent the state of Nebraska.
Republican incumbent Pete Ricketts is seeking his first full term following a special election in 2024.
Former union leader Dan Osborn, who ran in the 2024 regular election, is again running as an independent.
Primary elections were held on May 12, 2026.[1] Ricketts won the Republican nomination with 81.5% of the vote.
Although state Democrats endorsed Osborn, pastor William Forbes entered the Democratic primary amid accusations of being a spoiler candidate.
In response, retired pharmacy technician Cindy Burbank launched a primary candidacy supported by the party and defeated Forbes with 89.2% of the vote before dropping out of the general election in July to support Osborn.
Republicans have not lost a Senate election in Nebraska since 2006 when Ricketts was the party's nominee.[2] The last independent to win a Senate election in Nebraska was George Norris in 1936.[3]
Background
[edit]
Republicans have not lost a Senate election in Nebraska since 2006 when Ricketts was the party's nominee.[4] The last independent to win a Senate election in Nebraska was George Norris in 1936.[5] This election will be the first in which a state did not have a Democratic candidate in back-to-back US Senate election cycles.[6][7] Nebraska is one of three states (along with Idaho and South Dakota) where the Democratic nominee has withdrawn from the race, clearing the field for the independent candidate: Osborn.[8]

U.S.
Senate voter guide: Meet the candidates in the rollercoaster race
By Noelle Annonen , Multimedia Reporter
Sept.
23, 2026, 6 a.m.
·
Four candidates will face off in Nebraska’s U.S.
Senate race this November.
It’s been a rollercoaster of a race so far even months ahead of the general election.
There have been accusations of spoiler candidates, lawsuits over those spoiler candidates and candidates dropping out of the race.
And as the field narrowed following the primary election, it bloomed again with the creation of new political parties.
The race’s two frontrunners, incumbent Republican U.S.
Sen.
Pete Ricketts and independent candidate Dan Osborn, were joined by Chuck Conboy of the America First Party and Robin Richards of the Nebraska Working People party.
The two new parties were created this year by petition.
Voters will see a fifth candidate on the ballot, Mike Marvin of the Legal Marijuana NOW party, but he has since dropped out of the race because of health issues.
Ricketts and Osborn were the only candidates from the race who participated in a debate at the Nebraska State Fair on Sept.
1.
Osborn, who got on the ballot via petition, says he wants to break the two-party system, though Ricketts sees him as a Democrat in disguise.
Ricketts hopes to continue supporting tax breaks for Nebraskans, pushing the implementation of biofuels, such as E15, across the country, and ensuring safety particularly around the border.
Osborn wants to fight for working people, push for campaign finance reform and bring a unique and strong voice to Capitol Hill.
Conboy is building his candidacy on making both healthcare and childcare more affordable for Nebraskans.
Richards said she is in the race to give voters more options and support education and disability services.
Though Ricketts and Osborn are helping to garner national attention to the race, it’s also drawn attention for other reasons.
Cindy Burbank and William Forbes have both gone to court to get their names on the Democratic ticket in the race.
Burbank was initially removed from the ballot by Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, who took issue with Burbank voicing her support for Osborn on her campaign website and pledging to drop out if she won the primary.
Burbank filed suit in Lancaster County District Court to restore her name to the ballot and eventually won.
Once Osborn gathered enough signatures to join the race in July, Burbank dropped out of the race.
Shortly thereafter, Forbes sued the Nebraska Democratic Party to take her spot, despite receiving only 10% of the vote in the primaries.
But a judge ruled in favor of the party and did not force it to replace its candidate in the U.S.
Senate race.
Candidates from the America First Party and the Nebraska Working People party did not join the ballot until after legal challenges were raised and settled as well.
In July, the Secretary of State’s office confirmed both parties had submitted enough signatures by the necessary deadline to join other political parties on the ballot.
But the state Republican Party challenged the creation of the America First Party in court in August, calling the party’s language intentionally confusing to voters.
The Nebraska Supreme Court rejected that petition.
Meanwhile, the Nebraska Democratic Party and the national Working Families Party sued to block the Nebraska Working People party from the ballot, arguing that this party also was trying to confuse voters through its name by creating a false association with Osborn.
The Nebraska Supreme Court struck down this objection as well.
Now, both Conboy and Richards will join Osborn and Ricketts in the race for the senate seat.
Marvin of the Legal Marijuana NOW party also dropped out, citing health reasons.
He gave Osborn his support.
Marvin missed the deadline to remove his name from the ballot but said he will no longer solicit votes.
Republican Sen.
Ricketts seeking reelection
Ricketts served as Nebraska’s governor from 2015 to 2023.
Later that year, Gov.
Jim Pillen appointed him to fill a vacancy left by U.S.
Sen.
Ben Sasse.
Ricketts won a special election for the same seat in 2024.
He had previously run for the Senate seat in 2006 against then-incumbent Democrat Sen.
Ben Nelson but lost in a landslide.
“It is great to continue to serve the people of Nebraska,” Ricketts said, leaning back in a conference room chair as he met with Nebraska Public Media News to discuss his latest campaign.
“We've got the best place in the world.
We've just got wonderful people.”
Over the last three years, Ricketts said his main goal has been bringing Nebraska ideas and values to the rest of the country.
Much of that means cutting red tape and regulations that create long wait times for things like construction permits, food assistance applications or reimbursements for medical expenses for people with disabilities.
“I evangelize permitting reform and process improvement to everyone who comes into my office,” Ricketts said.
Ricketts said he has supported affordability through the Rural Workforce Housing Fund, hoping it will create more housing stock and, by extension, more affordable housing.
He also advocated for the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which, among many other things, cuts regulatory red tape.
